strengths: The dynamic, layer-specific composition of a learned LoRA bank is a sensible and reasonably original approach to specializing an editor for each visual analogy without test-time optimization.
The method is clearly motivated and technically accessible, with useful ablations over basis size, rank, routing activation, encoder layout, and CLIP versus SigLIP2.

Evaluation covers 100 nominally unseen tasks and 840 triplets, multiple automated metrics, pairwise VLM judgments, and a human preference study. The reference-pair experiment also provides evidence that the model uses visual demonstrations rather than only the accompanying text.
Qualitative examples span style transfer, object addition, background replacement, and appearance changes. Several examples preserve the source content better than prior methods.

weaknesses: The central comparison does not convincingly isolate the claimed benefit of a LoRA basis. Against the capacity-matched single-LoRA baseline, gains are modest: VLM accuracy rises from 5.70 to 5.94 and human preference is 57.6%, while preservation and LPIPS become worse. No uncertainty estimates or repeated-training results are reported for these aggregate metrics.

There is an important ambiguity in Eq. (2): defining A=sum_i e_i A_i and B=sum_i e_i B_i produces BA=sum_{i,j} e_i e_j B_i A_j, including cross-adapter terms, rather than the usual linear mixture sum_i e_i B_i A_i. The paper calls this a linear LoRA combination but neither acknowledges nor analyzes these cross terms. Equation (4) also appears dimensionally inconsistent given the stated shape K in R^{d x N}.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently established. LoRWeB and the single-LoRA baseline use FLUX.1-Kontext, whereas the three prior methods are described as FLUX.1-Dev based. The paper does not provide enough detail about retraining, prompts, inference settings, compute, or backbone matching to determine whether improvements over prior work arise from the proposed basis or from the stronger editing backbone and protocol.

The custom benchmark is not fully independent of the evaluated system: target transformations are generated using FLUX.1-Kontext itself or community LoRAs for that same backbone, and prompts for which Kontext fails are filtered out. This may favor a Kontext-based method and narrows the meaning of the claimed generalization to unseen transformations.

The human study is small and underspecified: it uses only 45 image pairs, omits the number of judgments per comparison, and filters cases where no method succeeded without defining who performed this filtering or how. The reported 68% intervals and lack of significance tests leave the slight 57.6% win over the strongest baseline inconclusive.

VLM evaluation carries much of the quantitative case, yet Gemma-3 agrees with individual human votes only 66.7% of the time. Describing this as 89.9% evaluation consistency by dividing it by inter-user agreement is potentially misleading. Results from additional VLMs or a larger blinded human evaluation would strengthen the evidence.

The learned routing mechanism is not directly analyzed. There are no visualizations of basis usage, specialization, diversity, stability across inputs, or behavior on held-out transformation families, so the proposed explanation that the basis spans reusable transformation primitives remains largely unverified.

Parameter and computational accounting is incomplete. Per-layer projections and keys add overhead beyond the LoRA bank, while the mixed adapter remains rank four despite being compared with a rank-128 LoRA. Reporting total trainable parameters, inference cost, memory, and controlled alternatives such as a dynamically routed rank-four adapter would make the comparison more informative.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: specifying difficult image transformations through examples rather than text alone. Dynamic task-conditioned adaptation is a reasonable direction for improving visual-analogy models.

The proposed system is conceptually simple and computationally practical: a CLIP/SigLIP encoder routes each analogy to a jointly trained collection of LoRA factors, while the underlying editing backbone receives the full-resolution image grid.

The paper includes several relevant controlled studies, including comparisons with a parameter-matched single LoRA, changes in basis size and rank, alternative routing activations, encoder-input layouts, and CLIP versus SigLIP2. The qualitative examples cover multiple transformation categories and are often visually convincing.
The authors supplement automated metrics with a human study and report both transformation accuracy and source preservation, appropriately recognizing that analogy editing has competing objectives.
weaknesses: The central state-of-the-art comparison is substantially confounded by the backbone. LoRWeB and its single-LoRA control use the editing-specialized FLUX.1-Kontext, whereas RelationAdapter, VisualCloze, and EditTransfer are described as FLUX.1-Dev methods. The large gains over these approaches therefore cannot be attributed specifically to the LoRA basis. Against the genuinely controlled same-backbone LoRA baseline, the reported advantage is comparatively modest: 57.6% human preference and 57.9% VLM preference. Stronger same-backbone controls, including a dense adapter or router with matched trainable parameters, are needed.

The claim of generalization to unseen transformations is not convincingly established. The custom benchmark is constructed from prompts derived from training tasks and outputs of community LoRAs built for the same FLUX.1-Kontext family. Novel wording is not necessarily a novel transformation. Manual verification and filtering are insufficiently formalized, and the unavailable original training split makes overlap difficult to audit. Results should be separated by source and transformation novelty, with a clear taxonomy and leakage analysis.

Text prompts explicitly describe the desired edit, so success need not demonstrate visual-analogy reasoning. Figure 7 offers only selected qualitative evidence that references matter. The paper lacks decisive quantitative controls such as text-only Kontext, blank references, shuffled or mismatched analogy pairs, and references whose visual details contradict the prompt. Consequently, the contribution of analogy conditioning and of the proposed router remains uncertain.

Equation (2) is described as a linear combination of LoRA modules, but mixing both factors as A=sum_i e_i A_i and B=sum_i e_i B_i yields BA=sum_{i,j} e_i e_j B_i A_j, including cross-adapter terms; it is not sum_i e_i B_i A_i. This may still define a trainable model, but it undermines the claimed interpretation as selecting a point in the linear span of LoRAs. The paper neither acknowledges these cross terms nor compares against direct mixing of LoRA updates.

The evaluation is not strong enough for the broad SOTA claims. LPIPS primarily rewards minimal change, CLIP directional similarity is imperfect for localized edits, and most conclusions rely on a single Gemma-3 judge. The human study covers only 45 image pairs, filters cases where no method succeeds, gives unclear per-baseline judgment counts, and reports 68% rather than conventional 95% intervals. There are no significance tests, repeated training runs, or uncertainty estimates for the aggregate metrics.

The basis interpretation is asserted rather than demonstrated. There is no analysis of routing weights, basis utilization or collapse, semantic specialization, interpolation behavior, or whether improvements arise simply from input-dependent parameterization and added router capacity. A generic mixture-of-LoRAs baseline and a hypernetwork-style baseline would help establish the specific contribution.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the stated code/data availability: the manuscript does not clearly enumerate targeted weight matrices, inference settings, prompt construction during training and testing, random seeds, evaluation sample counts after filtering, or full user-study assignment and aggregation procedures. Dataset provenance is listed, but the generated benchmark and its selection decisions require release for independent verification.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the paper has a plausible idea and promising examples, but the backbone confound, weak evidence for genuinely unseen transformations, absence of prompt/reference causal controls, and unresolved mathematical interpretation are consequential. These issues currently prevent a convincing attribution of the reported gains to the proposed LoRA-basis mechanism.

strengths: The paper presents a technically plausible and useful approach to visual analogy editing: a learned basis of low-rank adapters is dynamically composed from the reference pair and target image, providing task-specific adaptation without test-time optimization.

The motivation is compelling. Example-based transformations can convey appearance, pose, layout, or object changes that are difficult to specify precisely with text, and the proposed architecture fits this problem naturally.

The qualitative results are strong and diverse, covering style transfer, object insertion, background replacement, pose changes, and fine-grained appearance transfer. Figure 7 usefully demonstrates that outputs depend on visual references rather than only on the accompanying prompt.

The evaluation is broader than a single benchmark: it covers 100 unseen tasks and 840 triplets, includes a capacity-matched single-LoRA control, three prior methods, automated metrics, VLM judgments, and a human study. LoRWeB is generally preferred and offers a favorable edit-accuracy versus preservation tradeoff.

The ablations examine basis size, rank, activation, encoder-input layout, and an alternative SigLIP2 encoder. Results support the importance of using multiple low-rank basis elements rather than merely increasing the rank of one LoRA.

Implementation details are reasonably informative, including training duration, hardware, optimizer settings, encoder checkpoints, evaluation prompts, and sources of community LoRAs. Training for 10K steps on one H100 also suggests manageable reproducibility costs.

Although mixtures of LoRAs and routed experts are established ideas, jointly learning a layer-specific LoRA basis and router for visual analogy completion is an original and practically meaningful combination. The contribution is appropriate for the Algorithms/General category.
weaknesses: Comparisons with prior methods are not fully controlled: LoRWeB uses the stronger, editing-oriented FLUX.1-Kontext backbone, whereas RelationAdapter, VisualCloze, and EditTransfer use FLUX.1-Dev. The capacity-matched Kontext single-LoRA baseline is valuable, but the claimed state-of-the-art advantage over prior systems cannot be attributed solely to the proposed basis architecture.

The custom benchmark may favor the selected backbone. In-domain prompts are filtered according to whether FLUX.1-Kontext can perform the edit, and out-of-domain reference transformations are produced using Kontext-specific community LoRAs. Evaluation on an independently constructed or human-authored test set would make the generalization claim more convincing.

The formulation described as a linear LoRA combination is mathematically ambiguous. With A=sum_i e_i A_i and B=sum_i e_i B_i, the resulting update BA contains cross terms e_i e_j B_i A_j and is not sum_i e_i B_i A_i. This may be an intentional and effective parameterization, but it should be stated explicitly; it also complicates the interpretation of the basis and the capacity comparison against a rank-128 LoRA.

The human study is modest and incompletely specified. It covers only 45 image pairs, excludes cases where no method succeeded, and does not clearly report the number of judgments per comparison, participant allocation, or significance tests. These choices could inflate apparent win rates.

Much of the quantitative case rests on a single VLM evaluator, Gemma-3. The reported 66.7% human-VLM agreement is encouraging but materially below the 74.2% inter-human agreement, and re-expressing their ratio as 89.9% 'evaluation consistency' is potentially misleading. Results with another VLM or a larger human evaluation would improve robustness.

Several reproducibility details remain unclear, including the exact target weight matrices/layers, the full training split, inference hyperparameters and random seeds, parameter counts including routers and projections, and whether all baselines use matched resolutions, prompts, sampling budgets, and tuning procedures.

The basis-size evidence is not monotonic: N=16 is competitive with or better than N=32 on several metrics, while N=64 degrades. Thus, the claim that a large basis is important is only partially supported, and a stronger analysis of routing behavior, basis utilization, and statistical variability would help explain the mechanism.

The paper discusses failure on transformations far from the training corpus, but provides little systematic failure analysis or consideration of misuse risks associated with reference-driven identity, appearance, and style manipulation.

strengths: The paper presents a sensible Algorithms/General contribution: an input-conditioned mixture of low-rank updates that specializes a strong image-editing model to each visual analogy without test-time optimization.

The method is computationally practical. It adds only about 3.1% measured inference time over the matched rank-128 LoRA and is substantially faster than per-example optimization methods such as DIA and PairEdit.

The evaluation covers several complementary dimensions, including preservation/edit-accuracy metrics, pairwise VLM judgments, a human study, matched-capacity LoRA baselines, recent analogy methods, architectural ablations, prompt/reference sensitivity tests, and failure cases.
Qualitative results show useful transformations across styles, object additions, backgrounds, and pose changes, often with better source-identity preservation than prior methods.

The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and candid about limitations involving subtle edits, multi-component transformations, distribution shift, and the need for suitably controlled reference pairs.
weaknesses: The central empirical advantage over the most important matched-capacity baseline is modest: versus the rank-128 LoRA, LoRWeB changes VLM accuracy from 5.70 to 5.94 and CLIP directional similarity from 0.20 to 0.21, while worsening preservation from 7.99 to 7.87 and LPIPS from 0.27 to 0.31. Its pairwise win rates are only 57.6% for humans and 57.9% for Gemma. This does not convincingly support the paper's strong claims of substantially improved generalization.

The custom evaluation is potentially biased toward the chosen FLUX backbone. In-domain transformations are generated with FLUX and prompts on which FLUX fails are explicitly removed; out-of-domain examples are also produced using FLUX-specific community LoRAs. Moreover, methods receive the detailed generation/edit prompt, making it difficult to separate visual-analogy reasoning from ordinary text-guided editing.

The claimed learned basis of transformation primitives is not actually analyzed. There are no coefficient visualizations, routing statistics, specialization or diversity measurements, interpolation studies, or evidence that individual basis elements acquire meaningful semantics. A constant/unconditioned-router control is also missing, so the value of input-dependent routing is only indirectly established by comparison to a conventional LoRA.

The method description contains a consequential algebraic inconsistency. Equation (2) separately mixes A and B, whose product contains cross terms and coefficients e_i e_j, whereas Equation (5) defines the update as the sum of e_i B_i A_i without cross terms. The implementation used for the experiments must be specified unambiguously.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the exact FLUX matrices receiving adapters, the total trainable parameter count including the per-matrix projections and keys, LoRA scaling, sampling settings, prompt construction during training, and random seeds are not reported. Consequently, the assertion of capacity matching with the rank-128 LoRA is not fully verifiable.

The human evaluation is small and under-specified: it covers only 45 image pairs, filters out cases where no method succeeds without explaining who performs that filtering or whether it is blinded, and does not state the number of independent judgments per comparison. Only 68% intervals are shown, with no significance analysis for the narrow advantage over the matched LoRA.

The VLM evaluation relies on one model and its validity is overstated. A 66.7% human-VLM agreement is only moderate, and dividing it by the 74.2% inter-human agreement to claim 89.9% 'evaluation consistency' is not a standard or well-justified reliability measure. Conclusions would be stronger with task-level uncertainty, multiple evaluators, and a larger unfiltered human study.

strengths: The paper proposes a sensible and potentially useful extension of LoRA-based visual analogy models: a learned basis of low-rank updates with input-dependent, layer-specific routing. It performs one-pass inference without the expensive per-example optimization required by DIA or PairEdit.

The controlled comparison against a rank-128 LoRA using the same FLUX.1-Kontext backbone is valuable, and the paper also evaluates several prior analogy systems, multiple automatic metrics, a human study, runtime, alternative encoders, basis sizes, ranks, and prompt/reference sensitivity.

The qualitative examples cover diverse transformations, and several results show good preservation of the target image while transferring reference-specific visual details. Inference overhead over the matched LoRA is reported as only 3.1%.

The paper is generally clear and acknowledges relevant limitations, including dependence on relatively aligned reference pairs, failures on fine-grained or multi-component edits, and limited extrapolation beyond the training distribution.
weaknesses: The main empirical advantage over the strongest controlled baseline is modest. Compared with the same-backbone rank-128 LoRA, LoRWeB improves VLM edit accuracy only from 5.70 to 5.94 and CLIP direction from 0.20 to 0.21, while worsening preservation from 7.99 to 7.87 and LPIPS from 0.27 to 0.31. Its pairwise preference is 57.9% by VLM and 57.6% by users. No training seeds, uncertainty estimates for these aggregate metrics, or significance tests establish that this small gain is robust.

The evaluation does not cleanly demonstrate generalization to genuinely unseen transformations. Custom in-domain prompts are generated as variants of training prompts and only manually judged to differ, without a reproducible semantic-distance or task-disjointness criterion. The authors also filter prompts based on whether FLUX.1-Kontext can perform the edit, while many reference edits are synthesized with FLUX or FLUX LoRAs. This favors transformations already represented by the backbone and makes the broad generalization claim difficult to assess.

Detailed edit prompts are supplied at inference and often state essentially the complete transformation. The reduced-prompt experiment still provides the edit class, and there is no prompt-free quantitative evaluation or systematic reference-pair permutation test. Consequently, it remains unclear how much performance arises from visual analogy reasoning rather than text-guided editing. Conditioning the router on b as well as the defining pair (a,a') further permits target-specific routing, but the paper does not ablate this choice.

The human study is under-specified and potentially biased: it covers only 45 image pairs with 33 participants and explicitly filters out cases where no method succeeds. The paper does not report recruitment, per-comparison response counts, filtering rules, participant-level aggregation, or statistical significance. The dominant automated judge is a single VLM, whose human agreement is only 66.7%; dividing this by the 74.2% inter-human agreement and calling the result 89.9% evaluation consistency is not a standard validation.

The mathematical presentation of LoRA mixing is inconsistent. Equation (2) defines A=sum_i e_i A_i and B=sum_i e_i B_i, whose product contains cross terms and squared coefficients, whereas Equation (5) asserts BA=sum_i e_i B_iA_i. These are not equivalent without a different block-concatenated construction. Equation (4) also gives incompatible dimensions for qK^T under the stated shape K in R^{d x N}. The actual implementation must be specified precisely.

The capacity comparison appears to match only LoRA ranks while omitting the learned keys and separate projection/router modules for every targeted weight matrix. The manuscript does not report the number of adapted matrices, total trainable parameters, router storage, or peak memory. Reproducibility is further limited by the unavailable Relation252K split, absence of the exact custom images and generated outputs, and insufficient sampling details. Overall, the idea has merit, but the current evidence supports only a slight preference for rejection under the default Algorithms/General category.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and original Algorithms/General contribution: dynamically composing a jointly learned basis of LoRA updates provides input-specific specialization without expensive test-time optimization. The approach is intuitive, practically relevant, and distinct from both a single static LoRA and independently trained LoRA merging.

The method is evaluated against several recent visual-analogy systems, including a capacity-matched rank-128 LoRA using the same Flux.1-Kontext backbone. Comparisons with optimization-based DIA and PairEdit further demonstrate a substantial runtime advantage.

Results consistently favor LoRWeB across qualitative examples, VLM evaluation, and a human preference study. The most informative same-backbone comparison gives approximately 58% human and VLM preference for LoRWeB over the rank-128 LoRA, supporting a real, albeit moderate, benefit from dynamic routing.

The ablations are useful and reasonably extensive: basis size versus rank, softmax versus tanh routing, encoder input layout, CLIP versus SigLIP2, prompt specificity, and reference-pair sensitivity are all examined. In particular, the reduced-prompt experiments provide evidence that the model uses visual exemplars rather than simply executing the text instruction.

The paper is well motivated and generally clear, with strong figures and informative qualitative results spanning style, object insertion, backgrounds, and pose changes. It also candidly documents failures on subtle, multi-component, and strongly out-of-domain transformations.

The implementation and efficiency details are relatively thorough. Training uses one H100 for 10K steps, and inference overhead over a standard LoRA is reported as only about 3.1%. Dataset sources and the Unsplash license are identified.
weaknesses: The principal advantage over the strongest controlled baseline is modest. Relative to the same-backbone rank-128 LoRA, LoRWeB improves VLM edit accuracy from 5.70 to 5.94 and wins roughly 58% of pairwise comparisons, but has slightly worse preservation and LPIPS. Statistical uncertainty is not reported for the scalar metrics, and the pairwise advantage is close enough that repeated seeds would strengthen the case.

Some comparisons confound method and backbone: RelationAdapter, VisualCloze, and EditTransfer use Flux.1-Dev, whereas LoRWeB uses the editing-specialized Flux.1-Kontext. The rank-128 LoRA is therefore the cleanest baseline, and the paper occasionally overstates the breadth of its superiority based on less controlled comparisons.

The custom test-set construction may favor the proposed backbone. In-domain prompts are filtered when Flux.1-Kontext cannot make a meaningful edit, while many out-of-domain targets are themselves generated using Flux.1-Kontext community LoRAs. Evaluation on a fully independent, naturally collected benchmark with unseen transformations would make the generalization claim more convincing.

The mathematical presentation of LoRA mixing is inconsistent. Equations (2) and (5) effectively assert that multiplying separately summed A and B factors equals the sum of the individual products, but this is generally false because of cross terms. The intended operation appears to be a direct weighted sum of updates, or an equivalent block-concatenated factorization; this should be stated and implemented unambiguously.

The claimed capacity matching appears to count the LoRA factors but not clearly account for the layer-specific router keys and projection modules. Since a separate projection is trained for every targeted weight matrix, parameter counts and memory costs should be reported explicitly for all methods.

The human study covers only 45 image cases and filters cases where no method succeeds. The paper does not clearly state the number of comparisons per baseline or account for correlated judgments from repeated users/images. Moreover, describing 66.7% VLM-human agreement as 89.9% 'evaluation consistency' by dividing it by 74.2% user-user agreement is not a standard reliability measure and is potentially misleading.

The method still requires a textual edit prompt and assumes a largely aligned before/after exemplar pair. The manuscript demonstrates partial robustness to weaker prompts and misaligned pairs, but only qualitatively or on automatically simplified prompts; prompt-free evaluation and systematic robustness tests would better establish general visual-analogy reasoning.
